title: Champagne and the World
subtitle: What makes champagne itself, how the world's other sparkling wines are made, and how a warming climate is changing the picture.

episodes.title: What Makes Champagne Champagne
episodes.hook: Champagne is often spoken of as a style of wine, a celebration in a glass. In law it is something more particular: a place, together with a set of rules that every bottle carrying the name must follow.
cards: When the French speak of an appellation, they mean a named place and the rules that come with it. Champagne is an appellation d'origine contrôlée, a controlled designation of origin.
The place is a delimited area in north-east France, about 34,200 hectares of vines spread across 319 villages, according to the Comité Champagne's own figures for 2024.
The rules then describe how wine from that place must be grown and made before it may carry the name, from the grapes in the vineyard to the months in the cellar.
The first rule concerns the grapes. Eight varieties are permitted since an addition in 2025, and three of them, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, account for almost all of the region's vines.
The other four, Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris, are old Champagne varieties that survive in very small plantings, cherished by a handful of growers.
The harvest is governed too. Each year the region's interprofession, the Comité Champagne, decides how many grapes a hectare may yield for the appellation.
The grapes must reach the press as whole, unbroken bunches, and in practice that means they are picked by hand rather than by machine.
Pressing is measured with unusual precision. From every 160 kilos of grapes, no more than 102 litres of juice may go into champagne.
The juice is drawn off in two parts. The first and purest is called the cuvée, and the later, more strongly flavoured fraction is called the taille.
Then comes the method itself. The still base wines are blended, an art the French call assemblage, and bottled with a little sugar and yeast, the liqueur de tirage.
Inside the sealed bottle a second fermentation begins, the prise de mousse, or capturing of the foam. Its carbon dioxide cannot escape, so it dissolves into the wine.
That is where the bubbles come from. The Comité Champagne's own teaching material gives the pressure inside a finished bottle as around six bar, measured at 20°C.
The spent yeast settles as a fine sediment called the lees, and the wine rests on it, slowly gaining flavours of bread and brioche through a process called autolysis.
The rules set a minimum for that rest. A non-vintage champagne may not be released until at least fifteen months after bottling, at least twelve of them on the lees.
A vintage champagne, made from a single year's harvest, must wait at least three years from bottling, and most houses and growers choose to wait a good deal longer.
Only then does the sediment leave. It is gathered into the neck by remuage, or riddling, expelled in dégorgement, and replaced by the dosage, a little sweetened wine called the liqueur d'expédition.
Put together, these rules mean that champagne names a place and a promise about how its wine was made, and the word itself is protected in law.
Sparkling wine made anywhere else, however carefully, may not be sold as champagne in the European Union or in the many other markets that recognise the name.
None of this makes champagne the only fine sparkling wine in the world. It makes it one particular wine, and that is the spirit in which we will meet the others.
episodes.setup: France itself makes traditional-method wine far beyond Champagne. Next we travel to Alsace, Burgundy, the Loire and further, to meet the crémants and the rules that shape them.

episodes.title: Crémant, France's Other Traditional-Method Wines
episodes.hook: If you have enjoyed a glass of crémant, you have tasted wine made by the same method as champagne, from French vineyards a long way from Reims. Its rules are close cousins of Champagne's, with differences all their own.
episodes.callback: We saw that champagne is a place bound by rules, down to the litre and the month.
cards: Since a French law of 1975, the word crémant has been reserved for sparkling wines from an appellation d'origine contrôlée, and it was later written into European rules as well.

France has eight crémant appellations: Alsace, Bordeaux, Bourgogne, Die, Jura, Limoux, Loire and Savoie. Crémant de Savoie is the youngest, approved by the INAO, the French authority for appellations, in 2014.
Because each is an appellation, each has its own boundary, its own permitted grapes and its own detailed rules, set out region by region.
What unites them is the method. Every crémant is made by the méthode traditionnelle, with its second fermentation in the very bottle you buy, just as in Champagne.
The shared rules echo Champagne's closely. The grapes are picked by hand, and only the first 100 litres of juice from every 150 kilos of grapes may be used.
Worked out per kilo, that comes to about 0.67 litres for crémant against about 0.64 for champagne, so the two limits are close, with crémant allowing slightly more.

Every crémant must rest on its lees for at least nine months, against twelve in Champagne, and some appellations, such as the Loire and Bordeaux, ask for twelve months in total before disgorgement or release.
Pressure is set appellation by appellation. Crémant de Loire, for example, must reach at least four bar, while Crémant de Bordeaux asks for at least three and a half.
Champagne is generally around six bar, and a somewhat lower pressure is often described as giving a softer, more gentle mousse, which many people find especially easy to enjoy.
The greatest difference lies in the grapes and the places. Each crémant draws on its own region's vineyards, so a crémant from the Loire and one from Alsace can taste quite different.
In that sense the crémants are less a single wine than a family, sharing a method and a set of standards while each keeps its own regional voice.
For many years, sparkling wines like these could describe themselves on the label as méthode champenoise, the Champagne method, which seemed a natural way to explain how they were made.
European rules changed that. A regulation of 1992 allowed the phrase outside Champagne only where its use was already traditional, and only for a transition period that ran out in 1994.
When that provision was challenged, the European Court of Justice found nothing to undermine it, in a judgment given in December 1994, and the phrase has since belonged to Champagne within the EU.
The thinking was the same as for the name itself: a phrase built on the word Champagne was treated as pointing to the place, not only to the technique.
In its place producers use méthode traditionnelle in French, método tradicional in Spain and Portugal, metodo classico in Italy, and similar phrases in other languages.
Current EU rules reserve the words traditional method for wines made sparkling by a second fermentation in bottle that have spent at least nine months on their lees.
The word crémant has travelled a little too. Luxembourg makes Crémant de Luxembourg under its own rules, which date from a government regulation of 1991.
So a crémant is not champagne in a different dress. It is a family of regional wines made with the same patience, each telling you about the place it comes from.
episodes.setup: Across the Pyrenees, the traditional method has a home of its own. Next we go to Catalonia, to Cava, its own trio of grapes, and a classification rewritten only a few years ago.

episodes.title: Cava, Spain's Traditional-Method Wine
episodes.hook: Cava is Spain's traditional-method sparkling wine, made mostly in Catalonia and largely from grapes of its own. In the last few years its rules have been rewritten, and its labels now tell you more than ever before.
episodes.callback: We met the crémants of France and learned why méthode champenoise left their labels.
cards: Cava is a Denominación de Origen, Spain's equivalent of an appellation, and like champagne it is made by the traditional method, with its second fermentation in the bottle.
Unlike Champagne, Cava is not tied to one compact region. Its rules allow it to be made in several parts of Spain, including areas of Valencia, Aragón, Navarra, Rioja and the Basque Country.
Even so, the great majority comes from Catalonia, in and around the Penedès, where the town of Sant Sadurní d'Anoia is home to many of the largest houses.
Three white grapes sit at its heart: macabeo, the most widely planted, xarel·lo and parellada. They are Spanish varieties, and they give Cava a character quite unlike champagne's.
Macabeo is usually described as bringing freshness and gentle fruit, xarel·lo body and structure, and parellada delicacy and a floral lift, so the three are often blended together.
Other grapes are permitted too, such as Chardonnay and Subirat Parent among the whites, and Garnacha, Monastrell, Pinot Noir and Trepat among the reds.
Trepat, a Catalan red grape, may be used only for rosé Cava, which the Spanish call rosado, a small example of how carefully the rules are drawn.
For many years the best-known ageing words on a Cava label were Reserva and Gran Reserva, each promising a longer rest on the lees than a basic Cava.
In July 2020 the Cava Regulatory Board approved a new structure. It was published in Spain's official gazette in June 2021 and began to appear on bottles from January 2022.
The new rules divide Cava by its time on the lees. A Cava de Guarda must spend at least nine months on them, the same minimum that crémant observes.
A Cava de Guarda Superior must spend at least eighteen months, and the name gathers the longer-aged categories together: Reserva, Gran Reserva and Cava de Paraje Calificado.
Within that group, Reserva needs at least eighteen months on the lees, Gran Reserva at least thirty, and Paraje Calificado at least thirty-six.
From the 2025 harvest, the grapes for every Cava de Guarda Superior must be grown organically, a remarkable commitment for so large an appellation.
Paraje Calificado is the summit, a Cava from a single delimited vineyard, from vines at least ten years old, picked by hand and carrying a vintage on the label.
It is a small group that is still growing. Five more wines were approved in March 2026, bringing the number of Paraje Calificado Cavas to fifteen.
The reforms also introduced zones, so a label can now tell you that a Cava comes from an area such as Comtats de Barcelona, which takes in the Penedès, or the Valle del Ebro.
Not every Penedès producer chose to stay. In 2019 a group of them left the DO to create a collective label of their own, Corpinnat, with organic farming and hand harvesting among its rules.
Both paths reflect the same ambition, a wish to show how fine and how particular Catalan sparkling wine can be when it is given time.
Like champagne, Cava ranges from fresh, everyday bottles to long-aged wines of real depth, and the new words on the label help you find the one you are looking for.
episodes.setup: Not every celebrated sparkling wine is fermented in its own bottle. Next we visit the hills of the Veneto, where Prosecco is made in sealed tanks, for very good reasons.

episodes.title: Prosecco and the Tank Method
episodes.hook: Prosecco is made differently from champagne, Cava and crémant, and the difference is deliberate. Its second fermentation takes place in a large sealed tank, a method well suited to keeping the bright fruit and flowers of its grape.
episodes.callback: In Catalonia we watched Cava rewrite its rules around time on the lees.
cards: The tank method goes by several names: the Charmat method, the Martinotti method, cuve close, or simply the tank method. In Italy the name Martinotti is often preferred.
The names honour two men. Federico Martinotti, an oenologist in Asti, patented fermentation in a tank in 1895, by most accounts, and the Frenchman Eugène Charmat later refined the idea.
In the tank method, the base wine receives its sugar and yeast inside a sealed pressure tank, which Italians call an autoclave, rather than in thousands of individual bottles.
The second fermentation happens there. The carbon dioxide dissolves into the wine under pressure, and the finished wine is then bottled while keeping its bubbles.
The wine usually spends little time in contact with its lees, so it gains little of the bready, brioche character that autolysis brings to champagne.
That is the intention. Prosecco's grape, Glera, has delicate aromas often described as white flowers, pear, green apple and white peach, which a long rest on the lees could overwhelm.
The tank keeps those primary aromas, the fruit and flowers of the grape itself, fresh and clear, and that is why most Prosecco is at its best while it is young.
So the tank method is not a shortcut around the traditional method. It is a different craft, chosen to suit a different grape and to offer a different pleasure.
The grape's name tells a story of its own. Glera used to be called Prosecco, and the change of name in 2009 allowed Prosecco to be protected as a place name instead.
In that same year a large Prosecco DOC was drawn across nine provinces in two regions, the Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia.
DOC and DOCG are Italy's appellation ranks. DOCG adds the word garantita, guaranteed, and it is the higher rank, with stricter rules.
The historic hills between Conegliano and Valdobbiadene became a DOCG, and so did the hills of Asolo, and their wines carry the words Prosecco Superiore.
Those steep hills, with their small plots of vines on narrow grassy terraces, were inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage cultural landscape in July 2019.
Whatever its zone, every Prosecco must be made with at least 85 per cent Glera, which keeps the grape at the centre of the wine.
Prosecco comes as fully sparkling spumante, as gently sparkling frizzante, which may hold no more than 2.5 bar of pressure, and as a still wine called tranquillo.
A Prosecco rosé was approved within the DOC in 2020. It blends Glera with Pinot Nero, and it must carry a vintage on the label.
A small number of producers also make Col Fondo, Prosecco given its second fermentation in its own bottle, which shows that the grape can be read in more than one way.
Choosing between Prosecco and champagne is rather like choosing between a fresh peach and a slice of toasted brioche: two pleasures, each perfect in its own moment.
episodes.setup: Italy has a proud bottle-fermented tradition too. Next we go north, to Franciacorta in Lombardy and to the mountain vineyards of Trento, where the lees play the leading part.

episodes.title: Franciacorta and Italy's Traditional Method
episodes.hook: Italy makes far more than Prosecco. In Lombardy and in the mountains of Trentino, producers ferment their wine in the bottle, as Champagne does, and some of their rules ask for an even longer rest on the lees.
episodes.callback: We saw how the tank keeps the fruit and flowers of Glera fresh.
cards: Franciacorta lies in Lombardy, in the hills between the southern shore of Lake Iseo and the city of Brescia, in a landscape shaped by ancient glaciers.
Those hills are often described as a morainic amphitheatre, a curving sweep of stony ground left behind by the glaciers that formed it.
Its modern story is fairly recent. In 1961 the house of Guido Berlucchi, working with the winemaker Franco Ziliani, released a sparkling wine labelled Pinot di Franciacorta.
That wine is widely seen as the start of modern Franciacorta. A DOC followed in 1967, and in 1995 Franciacorta became a DOCG, Italy's higher rank, for wine made by the traditional method.
Its front label carries a single word, Franciacorta, which stands for the place, the method and the wine at once; the rules do not want spumante or the method spelled out beside it.
Chardonnay and Pinot Nero are the main grapes, with Pinot Bianco and a local white variety, Erbamat, also permitted in limited proportions.
The lees minimums are generous. A non-vintage Franciacorta must spend at least eighteen months on its lees, six more than the minimum for non-vintage champagne.
Franciacorta Rosé and Satèn need at least twenty-four months, a vintage wine, called millesimato, at least thirty, and a Riserva at least sixty.
For a millesimato, at least 85 per cent of the wine must come from the year named on the label.
Satèn is a blanc de blancs, made only from Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco, and bottled at a lower pressure of no more than five atmospheres, which its makers describe as giving a creamy elegance.
To the north-east, in Trentino, the Trento DOC was recognised in 1993 for traditional-method sparkling wine, and its producers present it together under the name Trentodoc.
Its vineyards climb mountain slopes, and the wide swing between warm days and cool nights at altitude helps the grapes keep their freshness and acidity.
The permitted grapes are Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Blanc and Meunier, three of them the leading grapes of Champagne too, with Chardonnay the main variety here.
Trentodoc asks for at least fifteen months on the lees for a non-vintage wine, twenty-four months for a vintage, and thirty-six for a Riserva.
Its story is usually traced to 1902, when Giulio Ferrari, inspired by Champagne, began making sparkling wine in Trentino, and the house that bears his name still makes it there.
In both places, as in Champagne, many producers age their finest wines well beyond the minimum, some of them for many years.
These wines are sometimes called Italy's answer to champagne, but the phrase does not quite do them justice, because each is shaped by its own hills, grapes and history.
Italy, then, offers two sparkling paths side by side: the tank, for the fresh fruit of Glera, and the bottle, for wines built around long, patient time on the lees.
episodes.setup: Across the Channel, a younger sparkling wine has grown with remarkable speed. Next we go to southern England, its chalk hills, and the Champagne houses that have planted vines there.

episodes.title: English Sparkling Wine
episodes.hook: England's vineyards have grown quickly in recent years, and its best sparkling wines are now poured with real pride. Their story brings together chalk, the grapes of Champagne, and a few Champagne houses that have come to plant there.
episodes.callback: In Italy we followed the lees from Lake Iseo to the mountain slopes of Trento.
cards: Sparkling wine is the heart of the British wine industry, making up around two-thirds of production in recent years, according to figures reported by WineGB, the industry's trade body.
Its leading grapes are those of Champagne. Figures based on WineGB data put Chardonnay at about 31 per cent of plantings, Pinot Noir at about 29, and Meunier at about 9.
Not everything is sparkling. Bacchus, a white grape widely grown for still wine, accounts for about 8 per cent, a sign that English vineyards have more than one ambition.
The vineyard area has grown fast. In July 2024 WineGB reported 4,209 hectares under vine, drawn from government data, and described that as growth of 123 per cent in ten years.
In other words the area more than doubled in a decade, and more recent WineGB figures, citing 2025 data, put it higher again, at a little over 4,800 hectares.
For a sense of scale, Champagne has about 34,200 hectares of vines, so Britain's vineyards, even at that latest figure, are roughly a seventh of its size.
In 2023, according to WineGB, the number of vineyards in the United Kingdom passed one thousand for the first time.
The chalk is the part of this story most often told, and it is easy to see why: the white cliffs of the English coast and the chalk slopes of Champagne look like close relations.
Geologists place both within the Anglo-Paris Basin, a vast basin of rock in which white chalk was laid down during the Late Cretaceous across what is now southern England and northern France.
So it is fair to say that the chalk of the North Downs and the South Downs belongs to the same broad deposit as Champagne's chalk.
It is less precise to call it the same chalk. The layers vary in age and detail from place to place, and the English and Champagne chalks do not match one another bed for bed.
Nor do all English vineyards grow on chalk. Many grow on other soils, such as sands and clays, and some much-admired English sparkling wines come from them.
Where vines do grow on chalk, the rock drains freely while holding water within it, a quality that growers on both sides of the Channel value.
Champagne houses have taken notice. Taittinger, with its British distributor Hatch Mansfield, announced an English project in 2015 at Chilham in Kent, on chalk, and planted the first vines in 2017.
The estate is called Domaine Evremond. Its first wine, a Classic Cuvée, was presented to the wine trade in 2024, with its public release planned for March 2025.
Pommery came to England in a different way. In 2014 Vranken-Pommery formed a partnership with Hattingley Valley in Hampshire, and the resulting wine is called Louis Pommery England.
Pommery also invested in a vineyard site called Pinglestone, near Alresford in Hampshire, while the wine itself is made at Hattingley Valley's winery.
It is tempting to read these moves as a response to warming, and some commentators do, but the houses describe them in their own terms, and we have not tried to guess their motives.
English sparkling wine is not a copy of Champagne. It is a young tradition finding its own voice, using Champagne's grapes and method alongside an English sense of place.
episodes.setup: Warmer summers are reshaping vineyards everywhere, and Champagne is no exception. Next we look at earlier harvests, riper grapes, and how the region is choosing to respond.

episodes.title: A Warming Champagne
episodes.hook: Champagne has long been a cool, northern place where grapes had to work hard to ripen, and that effort shaped its style. As the climate warms, the region is asking carefully what will change, and what it can keep.
episodes.callback: In England we met the chalk and the Champagne houses that have planted there.
cards: For most of its history, Champagne's worry was ripeness. Grapes from a cool climate kept high acidity, the lively freshness that sparkling wine depends upon.
Figures attributed to the Comité Champagne, the region's interprofession, put the rise in its average temperature at about 1.1°C over the past thirty years.
Harvests have moved earlier, though estimates differ with the period and the method. French agricultural researchers cited by Reuters spoke of about ten days over three decades.
Other figures, attributed to the Comité Champagne in the trade press, describe harvests starting about eighteen days earlier on average over a similar span.
Both point in the same direction. Where they differ, we would rather show you the range than choose the more striking number.
The 2026 harvest was a vivid example. Opening dates were published from 8 to 22 August, depending on the village and the grape, and the Comité's co-president called them the earliest ever.
Warmer seasons bring riper grapes. Reports citing the Comité describe potential alcohol, meaning the alcohol a grape's sugar could become, rising by about 0.7 per cent over thirty years.
Over the same period, those reports say, total acidity has fallen by about 1.3 grams per litre, and acidity is the backbone that keeps champagne fresh through its years on the lees.

In 2026 the heat was strong enough that the INAO, the French authority for appellations, agreed with the Comité a temporary exception allowing some wines to exceed the usual alcohol ceiling, up to 15 per cent.

The exception applies to the 2026 harvest alone and was said to affect only a small share of producers, and the Comité reported that average potential alcohol across the appellation stayed below 12 per cent.
One response is a new grape. Voltis, a white variety bred to resist mildew and powdery mildew, was admitted to the appellation's rules on a trial basis in 2022.
Growers may plant it on up to 5 per cent of their vineyard area and use up to 10 per cent of it in a blend, and the trial is to be reviewed after ten years.
Voltis is mainly an answer to disease rather than to heat, a grape that needs less spraying, so it is only one small part of a much wider picture.
Some growers are looking back as well as forward. Arbane and Petit Meslier, two of Champagne's old varieties, are valued for keeping their acidity even in warm years.
The region has also approved vines planted more widely apart, known as vignes semi-larges, which lowers planting density and is described as helping to preserve acidity and resist spring frost.
In research, a greenhouse called Qanopée, shared by Champagne with Burgundy and Beaujolais, is designed to bring new clones and rootstocks into the vineyards more quickly.
Many producers are also trying taller canopies that shade the fruit, cover crops between the rows, and other careful changes to the way the vines are tended.
Watering mature vines is not permitted in the appellation, so the answers have to come from the vine, the soil and the grower's choices rather than from irrigation.
Is the style changing? Some tasters find recent vintages riper and more generous, and some producers welcome that, while others worry about losing the freshness that defines champagne.
The honest answer is that it is still too early to say how far the style will move. What is clear is that the region is studying the question closely and with great care.
episodes.setup: We have travelled from Reims to Catalonia, the Veneto, Lombardy, Trentino and Kent, and back again. Last comes the honest account of what held up, what has changed, and what we left out.

episodes.title: Scorecard
episodes.hook: Every thread here ends with an honest account. This is where we gather what has held up, what has been overtaken by events, and what we chose to leave out, with our reasons, so that you can trust the rest.
episodes.callback: We ended in Champagne itself, with an early harvest and a region weighing what it wants to keep.
cards: First, what has held. Champagne is still a place and a set of rules, and its name remains protected, so sparkling wine from elsewhere is sold under names of its own.
The second fermentation in bottle is shared by champagne, crémant, Cava, Franciacorta and Trentodoc, and by the English wines made in the traditional way.
Prosecco's tank method remains a deliberate choice for a fragrant grape, and it stands alongside the traditional method rather than beneath it.
Time on the lees is still one of the clearest differences between these wines, and every appellation we visited writes its own minimum into its rules.
Next, what has been overtaken. Older books describe Cava with Reserva and Gran Reserva alone; since 2022, labels also speak of Cava de Guarda and Cava de Guarda Superior.
Older sources may describe Champagne as limited to its traditional grapes. Voltis has been on trial since 2022, and an eighth variety, Chardonnay Rose, joined the permitted list in 2025.
The figures we gave for English vineyards, from 2024 and 2025, change every year, so they will soon be overtaken in their turn.
And the 2026 harvest, with its early start and its temporary alcohol exception, is too recent for anyone to judge what it will mean for the wines in the glass.

Some popular versions deserve a gentle correction. England shares Champagne's broad chalk deposit, the chalk of the Anglo-Paris Basin, but not identical chalk, and many English vines grow on other soils.
Crémant is not a lesser champagne. It is a family of eight French appellations with their own grapes and places, sharing a method rather than a rank.
Prosecco is not simply a cheaper champagne either. Its method and its grape aim at a different pleasure, fresh fruit and flowers rather than the flavours of long lees ageing.
And méthode champenoise did not disappear because the method changed. The method lives on far and wide; within the EU, only the phrase has been reserved to Champagne since 1994.
Finally, what we left out, and why. We have not given one figure for how much earlier Champagne's harvests begin, because the estimates we found ranged from about ten days to eighteen.
We did not say how many zones Cava now has, because our sources disagreed, and for the same reason we left out the Reserva minimum that applied before the reform.
We left out the year of Eugène Charmat's own patent, which sources give differently, and the exact minimum pressure for spumante Prosecco, which also varied.
We gave no altitude figures for Trentodoc vineyards, because published ranges differed widely, and no lees minimum for Crémant de Limoux, where sources disagreed.
We did not list the grapes of each crémant, which deserve more care than a single card allows, and we did not claim any 'first' for Trentodoc or Franciacorta.
We have not explained why Champagne houses chose to plant in England. Commentators offer reasons, but we preferred not to put motives into the houses' mouths.
And we have not ranked these wines against one another. That belongs to your own glass, and we hope this thread gives you good reasons to pour more than one.
Thank you for travelling with us. We hope the next sparkling wine you open, wherever it was made, feels a little more like a place you know.
